en: One Scroll of the Ritual for Attaining Buddhahood through Recitation at Any Time or Place via the Yoga of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*,
translated by Tejin, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Daixingshan Monastery.
I prostrate and pay homage to Samantabhadra, the Wheel-Turning King of all Buddhas who has realized great awakening; receiving the name Vajradhātu,
he turns the wheel of the teaching’s command, which flows forth from his own crown.
The Great Vidyārāja Mahācakravartin, whose majestic radiance surpasses the many suns and who is surrounded by the seven treasures;
he is the Wheel-King of all the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartins, manifesting his wondrous and extraordinary form as soon as he appears.
All the assemblies of noble ones have vanished; because it is the singular essence of the Buddha alone, manifesting a supreme and peerless excellence, that Bhagavān,
by means of the light of his intrinsic wisdom, has formed a majestic solar disc.
Illuminating all realms without exception, destroying all darkness and gloom,
causing the mind of bodhi to arise; furthermore, through body, speech, and mind,
[I turn] the wheel of the Buddha’s activities within the entire vajra realm.
Its measure is equal to space, pervading the realms of all sentient beings;
it incinerates and severs their karmic obstacles and the fetters of false attachment.
To expound the uncommon Dharma, he bestows the crest-jewel and the seven treasures.
To cause the sudden realization of Bodhi, one should therefore take refuge in me.
This subtle and wondrous [work] has been compiled for practitioners of Yoga by means of the King of Great Teachings of Yoga, the Vajraśekhara.
The Gateway to the Principle of Attaining Buddhahood:
The profound and subtle piercing-measure that brings one’s own mind to perfect enlightenment;
Fully demonstrating through skillful exposition the signless and wordless Dharma— Vairocana Buddha.
The Yoga Recitation Ritual of the Supreme Secret Dharma of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King:
By practicing this samādhi, one realizes the Buddha-bodhi;
[composed by] the Dharma-transmitting Ācārya.
First, one should carefully examine the disciple: those who possess pure faith and certainty,
who have planted various roots of merit in the past, who belong to a noble lineage and are endowed with the marks and signs of excellence,
who are complete in filial piety, loyalty, righteousness, and virtue, and who deeply respect the teachings and revere the Triple Gem.
Thirsting for the Mahāyāna, upon hearing of and beholding the various bodhisattvas and their worldly skillful means,
one should not give rise to a mind of doubt regarding the work of transforming and delivering beings according to their capacities, but should joyfully cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
Courageously advancing without cowardice, protecting the Dharma and practicing the six perfections,
he relinquishes body, life, and wealth; without weariness, regret, or stinginess,
he seeks to study the Yoga teachings, constantly clad in great diligence.
Donning the armor of the great compassionate vow, Delighting in the joy of the three gates of liberation and the four immeasurables, With a mind of pity for all sentient beings,
one rescues them without interruption, Until they have attained Buddhahood.
If the consecration master perceives such a superior vessel for the Dharma,
he should first comfort and entice them through various skillful means by explaining the secret gateways of the Mahāyāna, as taught by all the Tathāgatas of the three times.
All are caused by entering this Dharma; having swiftly attained all-knowledge and provided various instructions,
he taught them to generate the bodhicitta and conferred upon them the Buddha-nature precepts and the adamantine, firm prohibitions.
When you have been introduced to the maṇḍala-cakra and received the empowerment and office, you shall be made to behold the assembly of noble ones. You are instructed in the samaya:
from now until the attainment of Buddhahood, do not forsake the bodhicitta.
Revere the ācārya as you would the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
All their words of instruction and admonition should be followed to the utmost,
Without seeking out the teacher’s faults, even when encountering conduct that appears afflictive.
Contemplate that the root of greedy attachment is primordially pure;
do not give rise to thoughts of resentment toward fellow practitioners.
Regard them with reverence as you would Vajrapāṇi, and even toward all sentient beings, you should never treat them with contempt or cause them distress.
All devas, ṛṣis, and others should not be worshipped with prostrations;
yet one must not fail to show them respect or treat them with contempt.
One should not intentionally ride over or step upon any object seen [there], for they are within the same ritual enclosure.
Upheld by all the noble ones, received directly from the ācārya in person,
together with the various ritual procedures, mudrās, mantras,
and the subtle samādhis of the wheel, vajra, bell, and so forth.
And all other ritual implements, for the sake of seeking accomplishment until reaching the rank of Buddhahood,
one should always maintain them and never abandon them even for a moment;
within this teaching, not even a single syllable should be disregarded.
It is said that one must not explain the teachings of the various deities to those who have not received initiation;
except for the original preceptor from whom one received them,
even fellow practitioners may not be taught these, even if they have already attained accomplishment.
As soon as it is spoken, it is lost; one immediately incurs various calamities and misfortunes, meeting an untimely death and falling into hell.
Therefore, always guard this samaya precept, as all Buddhas have proclaimed together.
All the noble ones maintain this; you should train in it without transgression.
Furthermore, regarding external rituals—washing, rinsing, chewing tooth-sticks, eating beans and groats, and applying fragrant ointments—one should ensure that body and mouth are pure and fragrant.
One should not consume pungent foods or impure mixtures, nor meat, wine, or any leftovers that have been touched by others;
one should always keep the body clean and wear pure garments so that there is no defilement within or without.
One should not grow long fingernails, nor dwell in filthy places that violate the teachings.
The "internal" refers to the six sense faculties; by means of the three secrets, they are purified.
The "external" refers to the various ritual procedures;
one may either bathe them with the water of the Dharma or, if external conditions are not complete, purify them through the Dharma alone.
This principle is most supreme; one should contemplate the syllable *Oṃ* as extensively explained below.
It purifies internal and external defilements without bathing, and it serves as a constant, pure garment.
Purifying like space, stainless as the dharma-realm,
with both phenomenon and principle in perfect accord,
the Tathāgata most highly praises the practice of the *kaca*— receiving the root deity from one's master.
Once the yoga ritual has been clearly understood and all doubts are dispelled, one should then practice with courageous diligence;
at all times and in all places, recitation will be accomplished. If, however, one is in a secluded and quiet place...
In famous mountains where one dwells at ease, or on the most excellent high peaks;
in places spoken of in various teachings or praised by the Buddhas;
whether in ancient stupas and temples, or in newly constructed meditation halls.
Purify the ground according to the instructions; having smeared it all over with cow dung until it is extremely fine and smooth,
then wipe the maṇḍala with ground white sandalwood paste, making it square or circular according to its size.
Arrayed are the various stages of the sages; when scattering them, they are adorned with flowers.
According to one's capacity, prepare the offerings:
unguents, argha water, incense, food and drink, lamps, banners, canopies, bells, and pendants.
Arrange the altar on all four sides. If there is an image of the Principal Deity, place it facing west within the room. The yogin faces east;
each time entering the maṇḍala, one should visualize that the Buddha dwells eternally in the world.
Placing the five limbs upon the ground, one should prostrate with full devotion according to the instructions;
then, one should again contemplate all Buddhas filling the realm of empty space,
as densely packed as sesame seeds, and immediately give rise to this mind.
I now universally prostrate and offer; immediately taking incense and applying it to the hands, one binds the mudrā of Universal Offering.
First, as usual, join the palms; then, at one's own heart, [apply it] immediately.
With all fingers, the right presses upon the left;
first, the fingers are interlaced to form the Vajra-joined palms.
All secret mudrās arise from this; therefore, it is named the "Treasury of Space."
Forming mudrās and reciting the secret mantras, place them upon the crown of the head and visualize that one’s own body makes prostrations at the feet of each and every Tathāgata; then,
relinquishing the body as an offering, recite the mantra for relinquishing the body.
I supplicate the assembly of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; please hold me in your mindful empowerment.
Reciting all the Vajras, through this mudrā and mantra of Amoghasamaya, may my own body become pervaded by their emanations.
In the boundless realms of the ten directions, within lands as numerous as motes of dust,
in the great ocean-like assemblies of all Buddhas,
there are those who are themselves like Karma-Bodhisattvas, standing before each and every Honored One.
Holding various articles of offering, one performs the act of surrendering the body;

all such matters receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). One repents, rejoices, and entreats [the Buddhas] to turn toward the conduct of Samantabhadra’s vows, as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other [scriptures].
Then, sit in the full-lotus posture; whether in the half-lotus or the wheel-lotus, always place the right foot over the left.
Straighten the body and stabilize the limbs and joints;
with the left hand palm up on the lap, place the right hand palm up upon it.
Immediately generate the mind of great compassion to rescue, benefit,
and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without exception; then,
recite this mantra for accomplishing bodhicitta according to your intention.
By reciting this secret mantra and generating the bodhicitta,
all karmic obstacles and hindrances are destroyed; one attains all delightful joys equal to those of all Buddhas and transcends all māras.
Unable to create obstacles, they should receive the vast offerings of all worlds.
Furthermore, one should carefully contemplate that the dharmas of the sense faculties,
objects, and consciousnesses are by their very nature originally empty.
Furthermore, contemplate the meaning of this verse:
"All things are like space, and space itself is without marks;
Because all phenomena are thus interconnected, they pervade everything. Recite these four lines of verse.
Whatever various objects are perceived, All are illuminated as empty, and that illumination itself is empty.
Through the realization of the essence of emptiness, One directly penetrates and beholds one's own fundamental mind,
Radiant and pure like the full moon, Free from both subject and object.
The self-nature is luminous, and the essence of enlightenment is firm;
furthermore, from within the lunar disc, there emerges a great Dharma-wheel formed of vajra, its spokes and rim all sharp-edged.
His color is like refined gold, radiating a pervasive and great brilliance that surpasses the suns numbering more than a mass of atoms; he abides upon the lunar disc,
his face marked by a vajra of extreme hardness, perfectly manifesting the fullness of merit and wisdom.
Benefit consists in the absence of conceptual proliferation; it severs and destroys all false attachments.
Its light manifests all-knowledge and dispels the darkness of ignorance.
It appears in the form of a wheel because its measure is equal to space.
All the Tathāgatas of space enter entirely into the wheel;
one then visualizes this wheel of wisdom transforming into the body of the Universal Illuminator, the Golden Wheel-Turning King, whose form and attire are like the full moon.
Adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence, he uses them to embellish the Dharma-body;
wearing a crown of vajras, with a wheel-garland as his primary ornament,
he is arrayed in various precious ornaments that beautify his body.
Holding the Great Seal of the Wisdom Fist (Jñānamuṣṭi-mahāmudrā),
seated upon a lion throne, a sun disk, and a white lotus pedestal; the Wisdom Fist Seal—
known by its middle name as Kucamari— is formed with the index finger pressed against the back of the thumb.
The Vajra Fist is thus formed: the right hand grasps the first joint of the left index finger, held level with the heart. This is called the Wisdom Fist Seal;
as soon as the three secrets are brought into correspondence, one’s own body becomes identical to the Honored One.
Able to enter universally into the Buddha’s wisdom, The attainment of Buddhahood is not difficult;
One obtains the wisdom, lifespan, power, and years, And realizes the Great Bodhi through all-pervasive conduct;
Therefore, it is named the Supreme Seal of Awakening (*Vijaya-mudrā*).
If one practices this yoga, even if they have currently committed immeasurable and extremely grave karmic obstacles,
they will certainly transcend the evil realms and swiftly realize bodhi; this is to manifest its supreme nature.
Because its meaning is profoundly subtle and secret, one abides here in this great mudrā-fist,
able to firmly grasp and maintain it; the ocean of the Buddhas’ wisdom-dharma is thus held firm without dispersal or loss, and one is able to accomplish all mudrās.
Therefore it is named the Vajra Fist. Holding the left index finger with the right hand throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle,
the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Crown, which brings all Buddhas into equal meditative equipoise.
Therefore, it is named the Fist of Wisdom (*jñānamuṣṭi*).
Furthermore, visualize the heart-moon disk adorned with a vajra-wheel.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Supreme Body Samaya of the Cakravartin at the heart, forehead, throat, and crown.
The mudrā is formed as before: with the vajra-pañjali firmly joined, extend the middle fingers side by side like the petals of a blue lotus;
then bend the tips of the index fingers and place them upon the upper joints of the middle fingers.
One should know the meaning of the mudrās: the thumbs form the *paryaṅka* (crossed-legs);
the middle fingers represent the body of the Buddha; they are named "Small" (*Kṣudra*) and "Accomplishing Radiance" (*Jvalanārcis*);
the two palms are the discs of the sun and moon; and on the exterior is the lion throne.
Therefore, he is named Tathāgata; this Vairocana of the supreme body-samaya is no different from the single syllable of the three-syllable secret mantra of the Buddha.
It is precisely through the seal and the secret mantra [that this is so].
Sealing the heart accomplishes the mirror-like wisdom; one swiftly attains the adamantine, firm essence of the Bodhicitta.
One should know that sealing the forehead accomplishes the wisdom of equality;
one swiftly attains the stage of empowerment.
Adorning the body with a mass of merit, when the mantra is placed upon the mouth as a mudrā, one accomplishes the wisdom of profound discernment;
one is then able to turn the wheel of Dharma and attain the Buddha’s body of wisdom.
Recite the secret mantra while sealing the crown of the head.

The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done realizes the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and is able to subdue those who are difficult to tame. Through the empowerment of this seal and mantra,
one's own person is perfected as the Wisdom of the Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu.
Vairocana Buddha, the body of the Dharma-realm of space:
then divide the mudrā into two; extend the two vajra-fists from the forehead to the back of the head, and raise the two index fingers.
Circumambulate each location three times; starting from the little fingers, let them extend outward like celestial robes hanging down.
Recite the secret mantra for all consecrations while performing this mudrā, and one will immediately receive [empowerment] from the realm of space.
In all Buddha-worlds, with vajra crowns, wheel garlands,
and silk ribbons, and for the sake of delighting the assembly of noble ones through the bestowal of complete empowerment, one should place both hands before the heart.
Clapping the palms three times with level hands, one should recite this secret mantra;
by means of this ritual of clapping the palms, the Wheel-Turning King and his retinue will become joyful and compliant, swiftly fulfilling the needs of the yogin.
The fruit of the siddhi of one’s aspiration shall be attained as a firm body.

Next, the ritual for making offerings is set forth: having made offerings to the Honored One and the assembly of noble beings, perform the vajra-añjali gesture according to the procedure previously explained.
Placing [the mudrā] upon the crown of one's head,
recite the mantra of the Great Bodhisattva Gaganagañja; one should then contemplate that from within the mudrā,
oceans of clouds of all manner of offerings flow forth.
Argha water and various fragrant perfumes; the wondrous music, song, dance, and playful amusements of the devas;
unguents, flowers, incense, food, drink, lamps, and the auspicious vase;
the kalpavṛkṣa tree and all varieties of precious jewels.
White fly-whisks, parasols, and pavilions; jeweled banners, pennants, bells, pendants, pearl necklaces, canopies, and flower garlands;
palaces, devas, men, women, and all that belongs to gods and humans—all objects of enjoyment.
In this Jambudvīpa and throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions,
all flowers growing on land and in water— those produced through the merit and aspirations of humans and devas,
as well as those born of transformation— possessing their exquisite forms and fragrant scents.
Furthermore, with all the essential fragrances of the various devas and humans,
blended with transformative scents— whether incense for burning or unguents for anointing,
of every distinct variety— their aroma is rich, wondrous, and pleasing to the mind.
Furthermore, one offers to all humans and devas the light of their essential nature,
their self-nature, and their various manifestations— this supreme and pleasing light that is worshipped by all the gods throughout the three times and the three realms.
The many varieties of distinctions, as taught in the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* and other secret teachings,
as well as in all the Mahāyāna sūtras and so forth— these are the vast implements of offering.
Having first made offerings to the principal deity and his retinue,
one then performs the equal invocation throughout all the worlds of the ten directions,
as far as the reaches of space and the dharma-realm, within every land as numerous as atoms.
Before each of the holy assemblies in the great oceans of all Buddhas, I abide making universal offerings.
Furthermore, observing the ten directions, I make this vow: "I now entreat all the Buddhas."
To those who have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma, may they swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma;
to those who wish to enter nirvana, may they remain forever in the world.
May such thoughts arise once more for the sake of all infinite sentient beings.
Sunk and drowning in the six realms of existence, they experience various karmic retributions due to the delusions of their own minds;
they destroy their Buddha-nature and remain unaware—this is truly pitiable and lamentable. How shall I now rescue them?
Again, he reflects thus: "The meritorious deeds I have accumulated should be applied to rescue and deliver them.
By offering scented ointments, I shall obtain the five Dharma-bodies; may they flow forth from this."
The five kinds of stainless unguents polish and refine those afflicted by the heat of suffering;
by offering flowers that utterly shatter all hells and sustain them against all fierce flames,
one shall obtain the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Furthermore, may this merit be dedicated so that the flower-pedestal of wondrous enlightenment may form,
radiating light everywhere to touch all; may it awaken those in the realms of humans and devas who are addicted to various sensual objects and oppressed by the constraints of the eight sufferings.
May the suffering of the transformations of celestial music be ended;
may the bodhicitta of all those devas and humans flourish.
By my offering of incense, may they attain the eternal bliss of Samantabhadra and the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddhas.
May they be endowed with a radiant and majestic countenance; may this fragrant cloud of incense be offered to those suffering in the cold waters.
By offering food, may they obtain the flavor of Dharma-joy, the bliss of dhyāna, and liberation;
may it be dedicated to those in the realm of hungry ghosts.
May a universal rain of all subtle and wondrous celestial nectar, food, and drink—
blessed sustenance— fall, so that all may be fully satisfied and forever freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst,
as well as the evil karmic habits of stinginess and greed.
By offering lamps, one attains the five eyes; Thus becoming a lamp of Prajñā that illuminates the asuras,
One forever severs deceitful hearts, anger, and delusion,
As well as the fondness for strife and the oppression of whipping animals.
Harming and devouring one another, may they attain a heart of compassion and always be reborn on the paths of humans and devas; May those in the heavens of the form and formless realms,
who are addicted to the flavor of samādhi, be liberated from these fetters of delusion.
I offer this argha perfumed water to realize the wisdom of equality and attain the rank of Dharma King over the three realms;
may these descending drops of vajra nectar be bestowed in return to bathe those who dwell in the waters.
Forever leaving behind the realm of animals, they swiftly attain the pure Dharma-body;
reaching down even to the Avīci hell, all the instruments of suffering in every hell are crushed like dust, and all become lands of cool serenity.
May all classes of beings suffering in pain be liberated and born in the Pure Land;
May they always receive joy through offering play, and may the Buddhas look upon them with compassion as they offer smiles;
May they obtain the sound of the Dharma by playing music, and attain supernormal powers by offering dance.
By offering a flask, one obtains the vase of the wise;
by offering jewels, one fulfills desires and acquires all manner of treasures.
By offering a tree of adornment, one obtains the Buddha’s robe and the tree of awakening; by offering a banner, one obtains a rain of jewels.
By universally relieving the poor and destitute, one obtains the supreme victory banner;
by offering bells, one transcends the hosts of Māra and gains followers; by offering necklaces, one obtains exquisite ornaments;
by offering flower garlands, one obtains a precious crown; and by offering the finest flowers, one obtains the countenance of a Buddha.
Furthermore, with this accumulation of merit, I dedicate it for the sake of the inexhaustible and boundless realm of sentient beings—
including those in the six destinies and four modes of birth—
extending even to my own body, mind, and speech as the three vajras.
The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind pervade the boundless realm of phenomena as vast as space;
may they be enjoyed with delight by all sentient beings, as I abide here in unconditional compassion.
Constantly upholding, rescuing, benefiting, and bringing joy to others, may I together with them dedicate this merit toward the attainment of great bodhi; may I realize the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Furthermore, one should observe in this way: all phenomena are empty.
The three spheres are non-existent; one should know that there is nothing to be attained.
Abiding in this samādhi, one can truly deliver others and obtain limitless benefit;
whatever is undertaken will be swiftly accomplished.
While forming these mental visualizations, recite the *Sarvottama-nānā-pūjā-kośa-sambhava*.
By the power of the empowerment of this mantra-seal of the Tathāgata’s vast ritual procedure, [the rite is accomplished].
Even if one's visualization is not perfected, through the truth of the Buddhas,
one truly accomplishes oceans of clouds of offerings, such as those described above, within all the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas.
Because it is established by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*),
one should next recite the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
Forming vajra-pañjali at the heart, lowering the body slightly to the left— this is the ritual for paying homage.
One should chant this Vajra song with a beautiful melody;
next, recite the secret words of *he-he*. Without changing the previous mudrā, join the vajra-palms, extend the arms, and place them peacefully upon the forehead.
This is the offering of the flower garland. With a refined and elegant tone, recite this while performing the aforementioned mudrā:
starting from the navel, gradually moving upward to the mouth, and then returning to the heart, rotate it clockwise.
Once the vajra palms have been joined, [perform the following].
Furthermore, by placing [the vajra] upon the crown of the head, it is called the "Advancing Vajra Dance.
Because this secret yoga is proclaimed through song and praise to the Tathāgata, even attaining Buddhahood is not difficult.
How much more so for those seeking all accomplishments! One should know why this is:
because all forms of pleasure are not equal to the bliss of the Bhagavān Vajrasattva; therefore, accomplishment is swift.
Next, one should recite the mantra of the Family Mother, Buddhalocanā, seven times while forming her mudrā at the heart. Then, one should seal four or five locations:
the four [heart centers], the forehead, the throat, and the crown; or, for five locations, the forehead and both shoulders.
Disperse [the light] at the heart, throat, and crown;
recite once for each location while forming the mudrā as previously described.
Having joined the vajra palms, bend both index fingers together, join the nails, and extend the thumbs upright.
Pressing the side of each index finger, it is said that through the empowerment of the Family Mother, the secret mantra of Locanā,
the deity and their retinue will all regard the practitioner with affectionate mindfulness; even if the yogin possesses [faults],...
Violating the rules of the Dharma and so forth— out of compassion,
one should not perceive faults nor oppress others. For those who uphold the secret mantras,
if they do not practice this method, they shall not attain even the slightest deficiency.
How much more so for one who violates the *samaya*: if one performs recitation without relying on the ritual procedures of *yoga*,
without facing the mandala or the *śarīra*, at an improper time or place,
or in an impure state, yet rashly binds mudrās and maintains the mantra.
One will certainly incur misfortune; within five hundred yojanas of all the venerable practitioners,
the Honored Ones will neither descend nor grant *siddhi*,
due to the majestic power of the Wheel-Turning King.
Because it would sever and destroy all dharmas, one must therefore always first perform this empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
For what reason are the ritual procedures for the Dharma not permitted at improper times or places when reciting mantras to seek accomplishment?
Possessing the majestic power of a Wheel-Turning King, you are the most supreme and peerless Honored One.
You should not restrict yourself by limits; descend to this untimely place.
Pure and free from conceptual proliferation, your teaching and command are inviolable.
Therefore, without missing the appointed time, one should immediately recite and invoke the gateway of the Yoga-principle:
establishing one’s own body as the deity through the construction of one’s own mind, one gathers the essence of all Tathāgatas.
Empowering oneself as the body [of the deity],
one dwells with the entire realm of space as a palace; situated therein,
one abides in the yoga of the deity, surrounded by the noble retinue.
The Great Maṇḍala is accomplished; for this reason, it is unimpeded.
Furthermore, because practitioners have not yet realized the nature of the Tathāgata as emptiness and signlessness, this King of Teachings within Yoga [is established].
The unique, equal, and pure— Contemplating the body as having the characteristic of emptiness is itself one's own tutelary deity. Through this resolute conviction,
at all times and in all places, One will attain accomplishment through recitation.
Again, form the previously described *jñānamuṣṭi* (wisdom-fist) mudrā;

recite the single-syllable mantra while visualizing the body as previously described. Within the moon-disc of the heart, a golden single syllable appears at the navel, and the tip of the tongue is likewise so visualized.
Thus, this syllable becomes a wheel; that wheel is a *cakravartin* (wheel-turning king), its color like gold and its form majestic.
It is surrounded by the seven treasures, with the precious wheel-treasure positioned in front, while the remaining treasures are arranged to the right.
The Jewel of Jewels, surrounded by an immeasurable host of maṇis;
next, the Jewel of Women, together with boundless female attendants;
the Horse-Jewel, the Elephant-Jewel, and the Jewel of the Lord of the Treasury.
Each leading their own retinue, an immeasurable multitude stands waiting;
the Vajra-holding General Unconquerable serves as the master, while Buddhalocanā,
the Mother of the Tathāgatas, dwells together with Ratnolkā in the eight directions.
Just as a worldly Cakravartin King is surrounded by a retinue of the seven treasures,
so too is the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣacakravartin surrounded by a retinue consisting of the unsurpassed jewels of the Buddha;
when one forms this mental visualization, [one attains success].
Recite the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*, and with each repetition,
contemplate clearly that from oneself the body of the Buddha is spontaneously accomplished; from every pore of the entire body,
all [emanations] as numerous as the atoms of the world-systems flow forth equally.
The body of the Tathāgata extends throughout the entire realm of sentient beings,
rescuing, benefiting, and bringing peace and happiness to all;
he manifests the play of supernatural powers to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma and subdues all Māras.
Causing the siddhis to manifest, with pleasing enjoyments and so forth,
they return and enter one's own body; remaining in samādhi with mindfulness until exhaustion,
for one hundred, eight, seven, or three [repetitions].
Furthermore, bind the *Vijaya-kāya-mudrā* and recite the three-syllable mantra twenty-one times as appropriate; then,
take the bodhi-beads and place them within the palms joined at the heart, reciting the secret mantra.
Recite the mantra of bodhicitta three or seven times.
Holding the rosary to the crown of your head, recite the heart-mantra of Vajra Speech;
by means of this secret mantra, the rosary is consecrated.
Having recited the venerable secret mantra, once one bead has been passed,
perform one thousand repetitions. With both hands at the level of the heart,
each grasping the five fingers in a fist, begin from the first bead of the rosary.
Recite once and turn the beads one time; keep the beads level with the mantra until reaching the mother bead (*mātṛkā*), then return. One must not cross over the mother bead;
to do so is a transgression of the dharma. [Perform this] ten thousand times, or one hundred and eight times.
The count of one is fixed as constant; there should be no increase or decrease.
Once the limit of the count is completed, take the rosary back, join the palms, perform the empowerment, and place it in a pure location. Venerate the rosary beads as you would the Buddha.
One should not lightly discard the touch. The *Yogācāra-maṇi-sūtra* states:
"The beads represent the fruit of the Bodhisattva; the interruption in the middle represents the severing of the thread of outflows (*āsrava*);
the string threading them represents Avalokiteśvara; and the central bead represents Amitābha Buddha."
One should not transgress this, for by means of the jewel one accumulates merit and swiftly attains accomplishment. Next, having presented the aforementioned offerings,
one again binds the Wisdom Fist mudrā and enters the previous samādhi.
Contemplating on a single syllable, one reflects upon its meaning:
that all phenomena are fundamentally indestructible, free from dust and untainted, pure like space; because they are pure like space.
All phenomena are indestructible, because all phenomena are not subject to destruction;
all phenomena are fundamentally pure, because all phenomena are fundamentally pure;
all phenomena are unstained, because all phenomena are not subject to staining.
Emptiness and purity are ungraspable; when contemplating the meaning of the syllables, the mind abides in principle through correspondence.
Not dwelling on the syllables themselves, they are of one identical essence, pure and pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Having attained the non-conceptual samādhi on the true nature of the Wheel-Turning King,
even for a single moment, through association with a pure mind,
one attains unsurpassed perfect wisdom; thus, the karmic obstructions accumulated since beginningless time are purified.
Suddenly extinguished without remainder, the Tathāgatas and Protectors of the ten directions all appear before me; may all my hopes and aspirations,
both mundane and supramundane, be fulfilled and granted as I intend.
Even in this present life, one accomplishes the body of the deity;
furthermore, by binding the supreme mudrā of the body and reciting the three-syllable mantra,
one contemplates the bodhicitta and reflects upon the gateway of the letter A.

When contemplating that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, Samādhi and Prajñā should be practiced together. For example, when contemplating the syllable *A*: As soon as one contemplates it, one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen. Because one knows they are fundamentally unarisen, this is called Śamatha;
Contemplating the actual nature of the syllable is Vipassanā.
This is what is meant by "the dual practice. All contemplations are like this.
Furthermore, bind the seal of the supreme body; at the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, perform a single snap of the fingers to open [the seals]. Recite this mantra of liberation;
by means of these seals and secret words, the assembly of noble ones shall be released from their bonds.
Each returns to its own palace. The practitioner of yoga reaches the stage of liberation.
Again, forming the Buddhalocanā mudrā and reciting the secret mantra of the Mother, one consecrates the body as before.
Furthermore, using the secret mantra and mudrā of the Invincible Vidyārāja from within one’s own family,
seal one’s own body at the five locations according to the previous method;
with the right and left hands, the eight fingers are interlaced within each palm.
With the thumb slightly opened and bent, and the little finger separated from the side of the index finger—
by performing this empowerment at all times and in all places,
one cannot be harmed by demons, enemies, tigers, wolves, or various venomous insects.
No evil-minded humans or non-humans can ever overcome or subdue the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata first attained Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree,
he used this seal and secret mantra to destroy the armies of the celestial Māras.
If one enters, it is easy; for this purpose, perform the wrathful Ucchuṣma mudrā with physical contact:
form a fist with the right hand as usual and extend the thumb to perform the consecration upon the five places as previously described.
By performing this empowerment, one enters all impure places where māras and obstacles find no opportunity.
Next, regarding the yoga taught in the King of Tantras during the time of recitation, it is that which is praised by the Tathāgata.
There is no time, place, or location where [the practice] is not performed;
one should know that it is practiced without interval—whether for four times, three times, two times, or even just once—at all times.
The "three times" refers to morning, midday, and evening.
Adding midnight makes four [sessions]; the two times refer to morning and evening, while one session may be taken whenever leisure is found.
From the beginning until the end, one should always rely on this ritual procedure, even if there is no mandala or a purified chamber.
Wherever one performs recitation, one should first visualize the syllable *raṃ* to purify the body and the site.
Then, by placing the syllable *āṃ* upon the crown of the head,
the fire of wisdom is ignited, incinerating the body and the site until not even ash remains.
Pure as space, as soon as one abides in this samādhi,
the heavy sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are instantly swept away in a single thought-moment;
this lady’s samādhi does not reckon with the characteristics of body or mind.
Furthermore, by analytically discerning form and so forth, one merely contemplates a single object;
through this empowerment of the Dharma, the two realms are purified into emptiness.
Within that very emptiness, one visualizes the syllable *A*, which becomes a celestial palace.
Just as in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, within the jeweled hall, one again performs the initial visualization as before:
the syllable *A* forms the moon of the mind, which in its sequence is no different [from the previous]; this is the non-empty essence of the Buddha.
Whatever is suspected of being impure, all is incinerated by contemplating the syllable *laṃ*;
by the power of this mantra of the Dharmadhātu-mind, it is purified as the Dharmadhātu.
One should know that this is the meaning of the syllable *raṃ*.
That which is called all phenomena (dharmas) Is fundamentally pure and free from defilement;
because all phenomena are pure, Purity and defilement cannot be apprehended.
The letter A is the bodhicitta, The source of the knowledge of all modes.
These are all the phonemes taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time;
there is no phenomenon that is not this very essence of the syllables.
As soon as one recites them, they are identical to the Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
By contemplating these syllables upon the eye, one immediately achieves the divine eye;
the remaining four [clairvoyances] are likewise fully possessed. This may be understood by analogy for all the sense faculties.
Even regarding iron and stone, one should contemplate them with focused mindfulness.
It can move and transform into gold; this nature constitutes the secret mantra.
The teachings of the Buddhas of the three times all extensively clarify this syllable;
its meaning is difficult to exhaustively explain, so I shall briefly set forth its general outline.
All other characters whatsoever are derived from the Sanskrit script;
they are not merely regional scripts. Once the recitation is completed, one should dedicate the gathered merit so that all sentient beings may universally [attain liberation].
Just as I am, there is no other; again, I pay homage to the Triple Gem, repent, rejoice, exhort, and beseech [the Buddhas].
Having gone outside, I shall turn the Great Vehicle, even if only for a single four-line verse;
I shall seal stūpas and cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds.
By means of this accumulation of meritorious deeds and the empowerment of the provisions,
siddhi will swiftly manifest. Furthermore, to perform the abbreviated ritual procedure,
first recite the syllable *A* to generate the bodhicitta.
The left foot presses upon the right thigh, and the right foot rests upon the left thigh;

this is the Tathāgata’s full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). One then forms the Wisdom Fist Seal (*jñānamuṣṭi-mudrā*), which is supreme for the body and for empowerment. Having clapped the hands, one further recites:
The Ritual of the Vajra-Union: Reciting the syllable Oṃ for offering, and further empowering the Family Mothers;
remaining in the Wisdom-Fist (*jñānamuṣṭi*) mudrā until the recitation is completed according to the previous ritual; furthermore, the explanation of the abbreviated ritual procedure.
First, using the heart-mudrās and secret mantras of all the Buddha families, seal the five or four locations. As for that mudrā:
interlace the eight fingers with the right over the left and join them together within the palms.
Holding both thumbs upright against the side of the right index finger, this mudrā seals the vidyā-mantra.
When empowering oneself with it, one’s body becomes identical to that of all Buddhas; this is the empowerment of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ).
Perform the recitation while forming the *jñānamuṣṭi* (wisdom-fist) mudrā.

Sit as before in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), or in the royal ease posture (*vajraparyaṅka*). Alternatively, sit with legs crossed, one leg hanging down, or even with only the knees upright. These are the three types of royal postures.
Alternatively, one may perform the *Samantabhadra-paryaṅka*:
the left palm supports the right leg, while the right foot rests upon the left thigh; thus the *Samantabhadra-paryaṅka* is formed.
These various postures may be adopted as desired, followed by the *vajra-añjali*.
Recite the syllable Oṃ as an offering; when the count is complete, again perform the *jñānamuṣṭi* (wisdom-fist) mudrā and recite the single syllable. During the day, use the family-heart mudrā;
at night, use the Buddha-eye (*buddhalocanā*) mudrā. Seal the five places to provide protection.
Furthermore, I shall again expound this extremely concise ritual for recitation for the sake of those practicing yoga who do not delight in many teachings or are pressed by numerous worldly affairs,
fearing that they might omit [the practice] if the extensive rites were used.
First, bind the Wisdom Fist mudrā; this is the empowerment of the supreme body.
Next, arrange the ritual of offerings; even if one then performs the recitation, nothing will be lacking.
If one further applies extreme urgency, [the result will be swift].

Fearing that there may be interruptions during the allotted time, simply perform the *jñānamuṣṭi-mudrā* (Wisdom Fist Seal) and recite the mantra of the tutelary deity seven or three times; thereafter, one may proceed as one pleases,
whether walking, standing, or sitting, and perform the recitation according to one's inclination.
If you hold a bead to count the recitations,
do not speak until the one hundred and eight have been completed; if you must speak,
visualize the syllable *Raṃ* upon your tongue, so that even speaking does not create an interruption.
Alternatively, one may simply bind the supreme body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) and perform the recitation;
this is also effective. Since no limbs are omitted, why are these two seals alone sufficient to accomplish the complete rite?
By merely forming the Wisdom Fist, one is able to gather all Tathāgatas and accord with their places of entry and abiding;
when this mudrā of the supreme body-samaya is formed, all mudrās are thereby accomplished.
The secret mudrās taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are entirely contained within this seal. Furthermore,
all Tathāgatas are gathered together in one assembly and merged into this single Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, there are no two distinct characteristics;
all Buddhas rejoice in this, and all Bodhisattvas reverently honor it. Devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans subdue themselves and take refuge in it. It is for this reason that [it is so].
Without depending on the assistance of various mudrās, one mudrā accomplishes all mudrās.
If one performs the recitation as usual, one should follow the extensive ritual manual;
one should not cling to this [concise] meaning and thereby give rise to a mind of indolence.
I have extracted the essential core from among all the yogas and the great secret tantras;
this concludes the ritual manual for yoga, the concise compendium of the principle for swiftly attaining buddhahood as a Golden Wheel-turning King.
Completed on the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the third year of Chōkwan at Shimyōin, Kenshūji. Recorded by Hōjō.
One copy completed.
